html:
In 1859 the small fishing village of Yokohama on Tokyo Bay was opened to foreign trade. It soon became Japan's main gateway to the West.

After Commodore Perry's visits, the treaty of 1858 with the United States named Kanagawa, on the main highway, as a treaty port. The shogunate feared clashes between foreigners and samurai on the busy road, so it built a new port at Yokohama nearby instead, and fenced it off.

Foreign merchants poured in. Raw silk and tea were the main exports, and Japanese silk soon fed European mills hit by silkworm disease. A Chinese quarter grew up, now the largest Chinatown in Japan. Japan's first railway, the Tokyo to Yokohama line, opened in 1872. Yokohama also brought new things into Japan: newspapers, gas lamps, bread and beer. The city was flattened in the earthquake of 1923 and bombed in 1945, and rebuilt both times. It is now Japan's second largest city.
sum: In 1859 the small fishing village of Yokohama on Tokyo Bay was opened to foreign trade. It soon became Japan's main gateway to the West.
